sense: find the answer to a problem or a puzzle

terms.gloss: solve, clear up (a question, a riddle)
evidence: Val. Max. 9.12 ext. 3: quia quaestiōnem solvere nōn posset (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “of difficulties, riddles, questions, ambiguities, etc., to solve, explain, remove”, from Quintilian, Seneca and Valerius Maximus on. Cicero uses dissolvere of refuting an argument. The everyday senses of solvere are to untie, to set free and, above all, to pay (see pay).

terms.gloss: sort out, settle (something tangled or difficult)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.26.2: ut ejus negōtia explicēs et expediās (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to unfold or unroll; of affairs, to disentangle and settle them (Lewis & Short). It also means to explain (see explain).

terms.gloss: get out of a difficulty; work out, explain
evidence: Cic. Pis. 74: haerērem, nisi tū mē expedīssēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to free the feet from a snare; so to free someone from a difficulty, or to get a matter straight. With a question, to work out and tell the answer, as in Phaedrus.
To find by thinking: a plan, a way, an answer (see invent).

phrases.english: because he could not solve the question

phrases.latin: petō ā tē, ut ejus negōtia explicēs et expediās
phrases.english: I ask you to sort out and settle his affairs

phrases.latin: heus! inquit, sapiēns, expedī quid fēcerim
phrases.english: “Come on, wise man,” he said, “work out what I have done”
